notes: NMC professional conduct appeal on incompetent lay advocacy; Wednesbury test and fairness analysis are clear throughout.

enrichment.short_title: NMC appeal: incompetent lay advocacy and adequacy of reasons

statutes_considered.title: Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1997

key_facts: A registered general nurse appealed against the Nursing and Midwifery Council's decision to remove him from the register following misconduct findings.
The case against him rested on charges of inappropriate conduct towards care home residents, including use of a stick and alleged assaults in a hoist.
He was represented at the Professional Conduct Committee hearing by a non-legally qualified advocate, Ms O, appointed through the Royal College of Nursing.
The appeal alleged that Ms O's incompetence amounted to a serious procedural irregularity and that the committee failed to give adequate reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 12 of the Nurses, Midwifery and Health Visitors Act 1997 against a Professional Conduct Committee decision, heard under CPR Part 52 rule 11.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the advocate's conduct was incompetent but did not render the credibility-based proceedings unfair, and the committee's reasons were adequate.
enrichment.ratio: On an appeal against an NMC disciplinary decision, incompetent representation must be Wednesbury unreasonable and must have led to irregularities rendering the process unfair or the conclusion unjust; where credibility was the central issue and the legal adviser remedied prejudicial errors, incompetence alone does not justify allowing the appeal.
legal_issues: Whether incompetent lay advocacy amounted to a serious procedural irregularity
The test for allowing an appeal where representation was inadequate
Whether the Professional Conduct Committee gave sufficient reasons
Whether inadmissible evidence of a patient complaint affected the fairness of the hearing

confidence.notes: Outcome, legal test, and key examples of incompetence are explicit. Some linked criminal advocacy authorities are cited comparatively rather than as central ratio.

notes: Complex Rosshill liquidation dispute; s238 transaction at undervalue survives strike-out but s239 preference claim fails on connected person analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Rosshill liquidation: strike-out of s238 and s239 claims against Sinai
key_facts: The liquidator of Rosshill Properties Limited sought relief under sections 238 and 239 of the Insolvency Act 1986 against Sinai Securities Ltd.
Rosshill had covenanted to pay £6 million to Sinai under a December 2000 compromise resolving litigation over ownership of Hayle Harbour land in Cornwall.
The underlying dispute concerned whether Ronald Smith or Philip Carruthers was the beneficial owner of Rosshill and control of valuable development land.
Sinai applied to strike out or obtain summary judgment on the liquidator's claim as having no real prospect of success.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application by Sinai to dismiss the liquidator's insolvency challenge, treated alternatively as directions, strike-out, or summary judgment.
enrichment.outcome: The section 238 transaction-at-an-undervalue claim may proceed to trial; the section 239 preference claim was held doomed to fail and should not proceed.
enrichment.ratio: A liquidator may pursue a section 238 claim where consideration given by the company may exceed value received and section 238(5) defences remain arguable; a preference under section 239 given outside six months requires a connected creditor, and a person controlling one director nominee is not a shadow director unless the board as a whole was accustomed to act on his directions.
legal_issues: Whether Rosshill received no or inadequate consideration for its £6m covenant
Whether the court would exercise discretion under section 238(3) to make no order
Whether the section 238(5) good faith and benefit defences were satisfied
Whether Mr Smith or Sinai was a connected person for a section 239 preference
linked_authorities: Phillips v Brewin Dolphin Bell Lawrie Ltd [2001] 1 WLR 143
Re Paramount Airways Ltd (in administration) [1993] Ch 223

confidence.notes: Interlocutory conclusions on sections 238 and 239 are clear. Full merits of the undervalue claim were not determined.

notes: GBH with intent conviction appeal on summing-up wording; Saunders and Brown & Stratton analysis is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: GBH with intent appeal: 'serious harm' summing-up challenge
key_facts: Following a pub altercation in Exeter, the appellant was convicted of causing grievous bodily harm with intent under section 18.
He assaulted Michael Lumley with punches, shod feet and a bite to the genital area, causing severe eye injuries and scarring.
The Court had earlier substituted immediate imprisonment on an Attorney General's reference that the suspended sentence was unduly lenient.
The appeal challenged the Recorder's summing-up for using 'serious harm' rather than 'really serious harm' and for inviting a subjective test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge, with a renewed ground on no case to answer refused.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the summing-up was not a misdirection and it was appropriate to leave grievous bodily harm to the jury.
enrichment.ratio: Omission of the word 'really' before 'serious bodily harm' in a section 18 summing-up is not necessarily a misdirection where the injuries plainly amount to grievous bodily harm; a jury question framed by reference to how they would describe the injuries does not necessarily import an improper subjective test when read in context.
legal_issues: Whether the judge misdirected the jury by omitting 'really' before 'serious harm'
Whether the summing-up invited an improper subjective test of grievous bodily harm
Whether the case should have been withdrawn from the jury

confidence.notes: Single ground of appeal and outcome are clearly resolved with detailed consideration of the summing-up passage.

notes: Section 69 maritime arbitration appeal; dominant cause and remoteness analysis favour owners and remission held futile.

enrichment.short_title: Maritime arbitration: recoverability of chain-arbitration costs for unseaworthiness
key_facts: Vrinera time chartered the m/v Vakis T to Eastern Rich Operations (ERO), who sub-chartered to Bao Steel.
Vrinera brought a spurious safe port/berth claim against ERO, which in turn commenced a sub-arbitration against Bao Steel on the same basis.
The tribunal found the vessel was unseaworthy at charter commencement and that bottom damage was not caused by an unsafe berth.
ERO sought recovery from Vrinera of its own costs and Bao Steel's sub-arbitration costs as damages for breach of the seaworthiness obligation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 69 appeal on questions of law arising from a London maritime arbitration award, with permission of Cooke J.
enrichment.outcome: The award could not stand on causation and remoteness; remission was inappropriate because the dominant cause of the sub-arbitration costs was the spurious safe port claim, not unseaworthiness.
enrichment.ratio: Costs of a chain arbitration are not recoverable as damages for unseaworthiness where the effective or dominant cause of incurring those costs was the owner's decision to pursue a baseless safe port claim repeated downstream; foreseeability alone is an insufficient remoteness test but the mechanism of loss need not be contemplated.
legal_issues: Whether sub-arbitration costs were caused by breach of the seaworthiness obligation
Whether those costs were too remote to recover
Whether the matter should be remitted to the tribunal under section 69(7)

confidence.notes: Legal error in the award and court's alternative outcome on correct tests are clearly stated. Quantification was not before the court.

notes: Attorney General reference on confiscation jurisdiction for compendious money-laundering conspiracy count; Hussain and El-Kurd applied.

enrichment.short_title: Confiscation jurisdiction after compendious money-laundering conspiracy conviction
key_facts: The offender was convicted on a compendious count of conspiring to convert or transfer proceeds of drug trafficking or criminal conduct.
He was acquitted on separate counts alleging only drug-trafficking proceeds or only criminal-conduct proceeds.
About £7 million was laundered through a bureau de change in Maida Vale between January and June 2001.
The sentencing judge declined to make a confiscation order, holding he lacked jurisdiction because the conviction did not satisfy the preconditions of the drug-trafficking confiscation regime.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 following refusal to make a confiscation order.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; the judge's decision was quashed and confiscation proceedings were directed to take place.
enrichment.ratio: A conviction on a single conspiracy count to commit an offence under either the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 or the Criminal Justice Act 1988 satisfies the precondition for confiscation under the 1994 Act because conspiracy is complete on agreement to commit one or more offences, even if the jury cannot identify which underlying regime applies.
legal_issues: Whether conviction on a compendious conspiracy count enables confiscation under the Drug Trafficking Act 1994
The effect of acquittal on the separate specific counts
Whether uncertainty about provenance of laundered proceeds bars confiscation
Whether double jeopardy considerations should prevent the reference
linked_authorities: R v Hussain [2002] 2 Cr App R 26

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and outcome on jurisdiction are explicit. Pre-POCA transitional complexity is acknowledged but clearly resolved.

notes: RAF Fairford anti-war protest preparatory hearing; crime of aggression and justiciability rulings are detailed but outcome on domestic defences is clear.

enrichment.short_title: RAF Fairford protesters: Iraq war legality and criminal damage defences
key_facts: Three groups of defendants faced charges arising from break-ins and planned damage at RAF Fairford in March 2003 to disrupt UK/US use of the base during the Iraq war.
They sought to rely on duress of circumstances, lawful excuse under section 5 of the Criminal Damage Act 1971, and prevention of crime under section 3 of the Criminal Law Act 1967.
The prosecution asked preparatory rulings on whether the legality of the Iraq war was justiciable and whether an international crime of aggression could be relied upon.
Grigson J held the war's legality was not justiciable but allowed limited defences based on belief in preventing ICC Act war crimes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals and cross-appeals from preparatory hearing rulings under section 29 of the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals resolved without needing a final justiciability ruling; the international crime of aggression is not a crime in domestic law for section 3 purposes, and the lawfulness of the war is irrelevant to section 5 and necessity defences.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3 of the Criminal Law Act 1967 requires a crime in domestic law; the international crime of aggression lacks sufficient consensus and definition to be translated into English criminal law; lawfulness of executive war-making does not determine whether section 5 lawful excuse or necessity is available, which depend on honestly held beliefs and statutory criteria.
legal_issues: Whether the legality of the Iraq war is justiciable in criminal proceedings
Whether the international crime of aggression is a crime for section 3 purposes
The scope of lawful excuse under section 5(2)(b) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971
Whether necessity requires the greater evil to be unlawful
linked_authorities: R (Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament) v Prime Minister [2002] EWHC 2759 (QB)
CCSU v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374
Hutchinson v Newbury Magistrates Court (2000) ILR 499
In re Piracy jure gentium [1934] AC 586

confidence.notes: Core rulings on domestic defences and aggression are clear. Extensive international law discussion supports but does not obscure the dispositive conclusions.

notes: Village green registration JR; jurisdiction, Article 6 and post-1970 class (c) greens comprehensively addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Village green registration: Commons Commissioners jurisdiction and Article 6

statutes_considered.title: Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000

key_facts: Mr Whitmey, a trustee of the Hereford Diocesan Board of Finance, sought judicial review of the Commons Commissioners' decision that they had no jurisdiction over disputed section 13 applications.
Mr Tunnicliffe had applied to register land as a class (c) village green based on 20 years' recreational use.
Registration authorities commonly resolve disputes by non-statutory public inquiry before amending the register.
Richards J refused permission for judicial review, holding the statutory scheme did not require reference to Commons Commissioners.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from refusal of judicial review; application to amend to raise a new construction point was heard in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Commons Commissioners have no jurisdiction over section 13 disputes, class (c) greens may arise after January 1970, and the registration procedure is Article 6 compliant.
enrichment.ratio: Section 13 allows registration of land that becomes a town or village green after the original registration period, including class (c) greens; section 5(7) does not extend Commons Commissioners' jurisdiction to post-1970 section 13 applications; registration authorities may decide disputes reasonably, with court rectification under section 14(b) or judicial review providing Convention-compliant oversight.
legal_issues: Whether section 13 applications must relate back to pre-1970 registration
Whether Commons Commissioners have jurisdiction over disputed section 13 applications
Whether registration authority decisions engage Article 6
Whether registration engages Article 1 Protocol 1
linked_authorities: R v Oxfordshire CC ex p Sunningwell Parish Council [2000] AC 335
R (Alconbury Developments Ltd) v Secretary of State [2003] 2 AC 295
Oxfordshire CC v Oxford City Council [2004] 2 WLR 1291
Bakewell Management Ltd v Brandwood [2004] 2 WLR 955

confidence.notes: Three main issues and disposition are clearly structured across three judgments. Some Article 1 points were not fully argued.

notes: Long Van Hoogstraten civil litigation judgment; contempt, freezing order and strike-out appeals allowed on procedural fairness grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Raja v Van Hoogstraten: contempt, strike-out and sequestration appeals
key_facts: Mohammed Sabir Raja sued Nicholas van Hoogstraten from 1993 over property loans, blank transfers and alleged fraudulent transfers of investment properties.
After Mr Raja's murder in July 1999, his son continued the claim alleging fraud and constructive trust remedies.
Mr van Hoogstraten was imprisoned following a manslaughter conviction relating to Mr Raja's death; that conviction was later quashed.
Peter Smith J found contempt for breach of a freezing order, struck out the defence, entered judgment and issued a writ of sequestration while Mr van Hoogstraten was in prison.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals from multiple Chancery orders including contempt findings, costs orders, strike-out, judgment and sequestration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals largely allowed; contempt findings, strike-out, judgment and sequestration were set aside and matters remitted, with some appeals making no order.
enrichment.ratio: A party in prison and unable properly to participate should not be found in contempt or deprived of a defence without fair opportunity to be heard; strike-out and sequestration are not automatic punishments for litigation misconduct where there is no real risk to the fairness of trial, and a freezing order made without a fair hearing cannot safely underpin such sanctions.
legal_issues: Whether contempt findings for breach of freezing and disclosure orders were justified
Whether defence strike-out and entry of judgment were appropriate sanctions
Whether sequestration should be set aside
The effect of the quashed criminal conviction on civil case management

confidence.notes: Very long judgment with multiple appeals, but Chadwick LJ's summary of conclusions clearly identifies what was set aside. Some interlocutory history is complex.

notes: Compulsory purchase injurious affection claim for bridge hoardings; Herring distinguished and Wildtree principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Hoardings during bridge works: injurious affection compensation claim
key_facts: Ocean Leisure occupied a shop on Northumberland Avenue affected by construction of the Golden Jubilee footbridges.
Westminster City Council erected hoardings around works and storage areas outside the shop from 2000 to 2002, narrowing public access.
Ocean claimed compensation for diminution in rental value under section 10 of the Compulsory Purchase Act 1965 as injurious affection.
The Lands Tribunal held the hoardings would have amounted to public nuisance absent statutory authority and awarded compensation in principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on a point of law from the Lands Tribunal preliminary issue decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; compensation under section 10 is payable for special damage caused by highway hoardings erected under statutory powers where the obstruction would otherwise be a public nuisance.
enrichment.ratio: There is no special rule exempting reasonably necessary temporary hoardings for statutory works from section 10 injurious affection claims; Herring v Metropolitan Board of Works is distinguishable because statutory undertakers cannot rely on private builders' highway rights, and substantial temporary obstruction of the highway causing special damage remains compensatable following Wildtree and Clift.
legal_issues: Whether hoardings for statutory bridge works amount to injurious affection under section 10
Whether temporary necessary hoardings are exempt from public nuisance liability
The effect of Herring, Lingké and Harper on compensation claims
Whether loss of rental value is the correct measure of compensation
index_terms: Herring v Metropolitan Board of Works
linked_authorities: Wildtree Hotels Ltd v Harrow LBC [2001] 2 AC 1
Herring v Metropolitan Board of Works (1865) 19 CBNS 509

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue outcome and historical authority analysis are thorough and unanimous. Quantification remains for the Tribunal.

notes: Leading PIDA good-faith analysis; predominant ulterior motive test for whistleblowing protection clearly established.

enrichment.short_title: Whistleblowing: meaning of good faith in protected disclosures
key_facts: Mrs Street, an administrator at the Derbyshire Unemployed Workers' Centre, made disclosures to a local authority treasurer and a management committee member alleging misconduct by the coordinator, Mr Hampton.
Allegations included misuse of work time, improper account arrangements and unequal application of equal opportunities policy.
An independent investigation exonerated Mr Hampton and criticised Mrs Street; she was dismissed for gross misconduct in January 2001.
She claimed automatic unfair dismissal protection under section 103A for protected disclosures, but tribunals found her disclosures were not made in good faith.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal affirming the employment tribunal's rejection of protected disclosure status.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; good faith requires more than reasonable belief in truth and is negated where the predominant motive is personal antagonism rather than the public interest purposes of the legislation.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 43G of the Employment Rights Act 1996, 'in good faith' adds a motivation requirement beyond reasonable belief in substantial truth; a disclosure is not protected where the dominant or predominant purpose is an ulterior motive such as personal spite, though mixed motives do not automatically defeat protection and workers may still pursue ordinary unfair dismissal claims.
legal_issues: The meaning of 'good faith' in sections 43C and 43G
Whether good faith is synonymous with honest belief in truth
Whether ulterior motive negates protection and what threshold applies
The relationship between good faith, personal gain and reasonableness requirements
linked_authorities: ALM Medical Services v Bladon [2002] EWCA Civ 1085
Central Estates (Belgravia) Ltd v Woolgar [1972] 1 QB 48
Darnton v University of Surrey [2003] IRLR 133

confidence.notes: Detailed three-judge analysis of good faith with clear test and application to the facts. Overlap with reasonableness requirements is acknowledged.
